 NEW YORK (AP) — A rebound for several influential Big Tech stocks is helping to lift the U.S. market on Tuesday despite a fall for Apple and mixed trading elsewhere on Wall Street.
 The S&P 500 rose 0.6%, even though more stocks fell within the index than rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 115 points, or 0.2%, as of 1:24 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.1% higher.

 The stock market has been shaky recently as technology and artificial-intelligence stocks have swung on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI. Several of the most influential AI-related stocks held firmer Tuesday, which supported the market, after flipping from gains in the morning to losses in the afternoon a day earlier.
 Nvidia rose 2.8% and was the strongest force pushing upward on the S&P 500 Tuesday. Close behind were gains of 3% for Broadcom, 5.4% for Advanced Micro Devices and 1.9% for Micron Technology.
 Apple was long seen on Wall Street as a Big Tech company that’s less dependent on AI. But it’s still feeling the effects of the AI boom.
 Memory chips for computers have become more expensive because of the demand created by the rush to build AI data centers. Those additional expenses are hitting Apple, which said it expects to make less profit from each $1 of its revenue during the final three months of this year.
 That helped send Apple’s stock down 1.7%, even though the seller of iPhones and Mac computers reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
 Palantir Technologies fell 2.2% even though it likewise reported a better profit than expected. The software company said it made more money working with U.S. companies than from the U.S. government for the first time, as U.S. commercial revenue soared 148% from a year earlier.
 Tuesday’s midterm elections may also be keeping financial markets unsteady, but history suggests they may not matter much for the broad market. Going back to 1970, the S&P 500 has had a positive return in the six months following a midterm election every time, according to Brock Weimer, an analyst at Edward Jones.
 Some on Wall Street speculate that a Democratic sweep of Congress this time around could lead to more regulations and restrictions on AI development. But Donald Trump would still be president and have the power to veto. And Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington, which it sees as offering less risk of transformative policies that could reshape the economy.
 On the winning side of Wall Street Tuesday were stocks of several companies that reported stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected.
 Celanese climbed 4.2%, and DuPont added 9.5%.
 Revvity jumped 10.6% for one of the biggest gains in the S&P 500 after the life sciences company topped analysts’ expectations and CEO Prahlad Singh said end market conditions are continuing to improve.
 Expectations are high for all kinds of companies to continue to deliver big gains in profits as the U.S. economy keeps chugging along, even with high inflation and elevated interest rates. That helped send the S&P 500 to a record high last month.
 An encouraging report on the U.S. job market said Tuesday that employers were advertising more job openings at the end of September than economists expected. That helped push the yield on the 10-year Treasury up to 4.95% from 4.91% late Monday.
 In the oil market, prices continued to swing. Brent climbed above $107 per barrel overnight before briefly dropping below $101 in the morning amid continued uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. It was most recently down 1.1% at $103.65.
 In stock markets abroad, indexes were lower across Europe and mixed in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6% for one of the world’s sharpest moves following losses for its two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
 Stocks rose 0.3% in Australia after the country’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate for the fifth time this year.
 AP Writers Elaine Lai, David McHugh and Rod McGuirk contributed to this report.

 8 gardening and garden-themed gifts for the holidays, from tools to smart tech
 Give the gardener on your list a little green this holiday season. From clever tools to practical essentials and even an indulgence or two, these eight gardening and garden-themed gifts will inspire, entertain and help them prepare for the next growing season.
 Inspired by traditional African keyhole gardening, Vita’s Urbana 4-by-4-foot Keyhole Composting Garden combines a vegetable garden and composter into a single space. Place the raised bed on grass or soil. Add kitchen scraps to the compost basket at its center, and they’ll decompose naturally to nourish the surrounding plants, help retain soil moisture and reduce watering needs. Made from BPA- and phthalate-free PVC, the lightweight bed assembles easily without tools or screws. The company also gives back by supporting sustainable gardening programs in Africa and around the world. $239.99.
 A cross between a long-handled shovel and a handheld trowel, Sneeboer’s Great Dixter Planting Spade is the Goldilocks of gardening tools. Perfect for digging when you’re on your knees, the tool also has two side-by-side handles for comfortable maneuverability. Its small size makes it easier to work in established gardens without disturbing surrounding plants. The Dutch-made, heirloom-quality tool’s hand-forged, stainless-steel blade is angled and curved to scoop soil efficiently; its unfinished, 16½-inch (42 centimeters) ash hardwood handle is replaceable, ensuring a lifetime of use. $109.
 The tomato grower on your list might appreciate some liquid holiday cheer to celebrate their past (and future) harvests. Crop Tomato Organic Vodka is an award-winning, USDA-certified organic spirit that’s gluten-free, distilled from non-GMO corn harvested in Minnesota, and infused with the essence of vine-ripened tomatoes. With the flavor profile of a savory, garden-fresh tomato, it’s well-suited for a Bloody Mary, martini or a cocktail of your own creation (fresh basil, anyone?). Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price $34.99 for a standard bottle.
 Sure, you can use sticks or moss poles to support your climbing houseplants, or you can make a decorative statement with a Treleaf trellis. Made in Atlanta from locally sourced materials, each nature-inspired support is a work of art. Available in 13 designs, in finished or unfinished wood, including modular options you can extend as your plant grows. $24-$45.
 Get up close and personal with backyard birds as they bathe, drink and splash in the Birdfy Bath Pro solar-powered smart birdbath. Its dual-lens camera is positioned for optimal viewing and streams live to your phone via a free app. Built-in artificial intelligence identifies more than 6,000 bird species, and an optional paid membership provides additional benefits. The integrated solar fountain includes interchangeable spray nozzles and a shut-off feature to conserve water. Around $259.99 with stand; $199 without.
 The Stihl BRA 200 battery-powered backpack leaf blower will clean up your garden without noise — or smelly, polluting gas fumes. The blower delivers consistent airflow, with an easily handled lightweight, ergonomic design that lets you lock the throttle at any position to reduce hand strain. And it operates at just 64 decibels — quieter than an average conversation. $729.99.
 Mosquito repellant might not be on their wish list, but your gardening friends will appreciate your practicality every time they head outdoors wearing your gift during buggy season. Each Parakito wristband comes with two refills that use a blend of seven natural essential oils, promising 15 days of protection apiece. It's available in a multitude of patterns and solid colors in four sizes, including one for kids. Made in France of adjustable neoprene, the wristbands can also be worn on ankles. $19.99; additional refills are sold in sets of two for $13.
 Houseplants die all the time, but houseplant parents don’t always know why, or how to prevent it. The LeafyPod uses artificial intelligence to teach them how to care for their specific plant. After potting up a plant in the smart container, filling its reservoir with water and downloading the free app, users upload a photo for identification. The pot uses sensors to track soil moisture, then releases the right amount of water at the right time. It monitors light levels, humidity and room temperature, then communicates its findings to the app, which alerts you when the plant needs attention. $145.
 This gift guide originally published Nov. 2. It was updated Nov. 3 to reflect changes to the Birdfy Bath Pro's subscription model.
